comments.comment: … Just as the tabernacle was constructed according to Moses so that the services might take place (Heb 9:11), so this tabernacle, the composition of grace, is greater, the body of Christ having Christ as head. …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Under the law the service worked through the blood of another and only by a pattern and shadow, but Christ saved those under heaven by his own blood.
comments.comment:
… The most wise Paul has written to us: 'But Christ, having come as a High Priest of the things about to come through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands—that is, not of this creation—neither through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, entered once into the holy places, having found eternal redemption' (Hebrews 9:11-12). For the power of the service was being exercised through the blood of another by those who performed divine service according to the law.

For they have worshiped the heavenly things only by a pattern and a shadow.

But Christ did not do so—and indeed much more is required—for he has saved those under heaven by his own blood …
comments.selected_reason: Contrasts the old service with Christ's entering by his own blood.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son of God has his own blood because he was also styled son of man, and he gave it as exchange for the life of all.
comments.comment: … “But Christ, having arrived as high priest of the coming goods, through the greater and more perfect tent, not handmade… and through his own blood entered once for all into the holies, having found eternal redemption.” (Hebrews 9:11–12) How then would the one at the Father’s right as God be said to have his own blood, unless we have believed that the Son from God the Father by nature has also been styled son of man, and giving his own blood as exchange for the life of all, found for the world this redemption unto the age?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: If there is benefit in the types and the shadow brings salvation, the blood of Christ must do far more.
comments.comment: … For he is our cleansing, the washing away of every stain, and the giver of sanctification. ‘For you shall sprinkle them,’ it says, ‘with water of purification’ (Numbers 8:7). This is just what the wise Paul made plain when he wrote: ‘For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who have been defiled, sanctify for the purity of the flesh, how much more the blood of Christ’ (Hebrews 9:13–14). And the saying is true. For if there is benefit in the types, and the shadow brings salvation, how could the truth, that is, the blood of Christ, not do so far more? …
comments.selected_reason: Gives the reasoning behind 'how much more' in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Christ sprinkles us with his own blood, cleansing not only the flesh as the rites of the law did but our conscience from dead works.
comments.comment: … As far as the type falls short of the truth, so far, I think, do those who serve it come behind those who minister the truth as priests. For Christ sprinkles us with His own blood, and not only for “the purity of the flesh,” as the rites of the law certainly did; rather He cleanses “our conscience from dead works” (Hebrews 9:13–14) and frees us from transgression. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The blood of a common human would do no more than the blood of goats, but the blood of the one who is from God by nature cleanses believers from dead works.
comments.comment: … If Christ is not true God, what is the benefit through his blood? Or how will he cleanse our conscience from dead works? What more does the blood of a common human have than the blood of goats? Nothing at all — except that one is of an irrational animal and the other of a rational one. But since the one who is from God by nature took flesh and laid down his own blood for all, by that very fact he can cleanse those who believe in him, free them from dead works, and lead them into worship of God. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Dead works are those through which the soul is put to death by turning toward the things of the flesh and the world.
comments.comment: … We who are being made alive in Christ (and by making alive I mean the spiritual kind) must depart from dead works (Hebrews 9:14) and go as far from them as we can. These, I think, would be the works through which the soul is put to death and the mind grows cold, when it has turned without restraint toward the things of the flesh and of the world. …
comments.selected_reason: Says what the 'dead works' are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The tabernacle was a type of the whole world, and the things here were antitypes of the true ones.
comments.comment: And to show that this is not our own speculation but that the tabernacle was constructed as a type of the whole world, listen to what Paul says when he speaks of Christ ascending into heaven: “For Christ did not enter a holy place made by hands, antitypes of the true ones” (Hebrews 9:24). He shows that the things here were antitypes of the true ones. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'antitypes of the true ones' means.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Christ appears for us in a new way, no longer as a bare Word but in our nature, presenting us in the Father's eyes as in himself.
comments.comment: … And he appears now for us before God’s face—in what manner? Was he not always apparent even before the incarnation? Therefore he appears in a new way: no longer a naked and fleshless Word, as indeed he also was in the beginning (John 1:1), but in the form and nature that is as we are. For we say that thus he has now appeared for us and, as it were, led human nature into the sight of God and Father, although it had come into aversion through the transgression in Adam (Romans 5:12–19). So then he presents us in the Father’s eyes, as in himself and first, insofar as he has appeared as human, so that he might bring us near to the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that he appears before God's face for us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Christ came at the end, when this age had all but reached its setting, and through him we have washed off the filth of sin.
comments.comment: … Thus the saying that the defiled man is unclean until evening would point very well to the time of Christ’s coming. For Christ came at the end (Hebrews 9:26), when this age had all but reached its very setting; through him and in him we have washed off all the filth that comes from sin, and we who were held fast by our offenses have been set free from charges both small and great. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Paul's word that all men die once would be false if Elijah and Enoch remain in their bodies, so their mortal part must be set aside by the secret word of God.
comments.comment: … It is proper to observe here how what is said by Paul, 'And just as it is appointed for men to die once' (Heb 9:27), is made true. For if these, I say Elijah and Enoch, having been taken up, are to be with their thickest bodies even now and throughout the whole age, then the word of the wise and holy Paul concerning the necessity of all men dying is false. But it is not false. Therefore, what is set forth requires a theory, even if not in the way accustomed, that although other men have shared in death now, it must be understood that their mortal part is to be set aside according to the secret word of God, so that they might possess the fleshy life. For if the Savior is the 'firstborn from the dead' (Col 1:18), He would be the firstborn of these. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The law's shadow is no match for the Gospel's light, which reaches the whole world.
comments.comment: …For in spiritual brightness the shadow in the law (Hebrews 10:1) is in no way equal to the decrees of the Gospel. These flash their light around the whole inhabited world, while the shadow was a token for those of Israel alone. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The old sacrifices were fulfilled, not condemned, when Christ, whom they foreshadowed, came.
comments.comment: …No one should be troubled here by seeing that the old sacrificial rites ceased in the age of the New Testament. Virtues and sacrificial victims are not governed by the same principle: commands are enduring; sacrifices are temporary. Yet when Christ came, whom the ancient sacrifices foreshadowed, what had been established was fulfilled, not condemned. Those observances are not denounced as having been practiced in their proper times; they came to rest when the perfection promised through their service arrived (Matthew 5:17) (Hebrews 10:1).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly why the law's shadows ended when Christ came.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Paul's "cannot" means impossible: animal blood has no power to cleanse the passions of a rational soul.
comments.comment: …“Cannot” is said both of things that are impossible and of things that are not permitted. Not being able is one thing; not being permitted is another. About impossible things Paul speaks this way: “The blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). For the blood of an irrational animal does not cleanse the passions of a rational soul. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why animal blood could not take away sins.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Even consecrated priests had to wash before ministering, so the law's worship fell short of cleansing until baptism was added.
comments.comment: …Now see how Aaron, though he was holy according to the law, and those appointed to minister with him as well, first wash their hands and feet with water, and only then set their hands to the sacred tasks and run into the Holy of Holies free from fear. Here, I think, the law shows plainly and clearly, and the fact itself all but cries out, that even one who seems to be consecrated according to the law is unconsecrated before God unless he washes in the water, and that the power of worship under the law is not enough for cleansing. … And the most wise Paul writes that it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). So the law falls short of sanctification unless saving baptism is added for those who thirst for closeness to God. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Christ offered himself because the type's worship could not justify, so a second covenant was sought.
comments.comment: …He offered himself for us, since the worship of the type was powerless to achieve justification, for 'it was impossible to take away the sin of these' goats and calves (Hebrews 10:4); from this, a second covenant was sought, because the first did not possess blamelessness within itself. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Word entered the world by becoming part of it, taking the body the Father prepared, to be an exchange for the life of all.
comments.comment:
…Knowing the will of God and the Father, the Son who is from Him according to nature, has become a man for all of us, both offering himself and performing divine service to Him.

The blessed Paul, who was no false-speaker, would become a witness to this for us; for he said again concerning him, 'Therefore, entering into the world, he says: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me' (Hebrews 10:5).

'Burnt offerings and concerning sin you did not seek' (Hebrews 10:6); then I said, 'Behold, I have come, as it is written of me at the head of a book, to do your will' (Hebrews 10:7). Who then is it that is entering into the world? And how is it said that he has fully entered in? Is it not that he previously existed outside of him, as if exiled? The Word from God has indeed entered into this world, not in a local sense but rather naturally, when he himself became a part of the world, having prepared for him the body of God and Father, so that he might become an exchange for the life of all, having died in the flesh according to the writings. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since the Son said God wanted a prepared body and not offerings, clinging to the law's sacrifices is now sin.
comments.comment: …So it is sin and defilement, now that Christ has been revealed and the time of the law and the prophets has gone by, to cling to worship as in shadows, and to attempt to bring to God a sheep, or fat, or frankincense, even though the Son says plainly to God the Father: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure. Then I said: See, I have come, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book, to do your will, O God’ (Hebrews 10:5–7; Psalm 40:6–8). For the Son, offering himself up for us as a spotless victim (Hebrews 9:14), put a stop to the things of the law, which could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:11); for Christ is the end of the law and the prophets (Romans 10:4). …
comments.selected_reason: Shows why the Son's words in these verses end the old offerings.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ entered heaven to appear before God for us, setting us in his own place, so in him we have access and boldness to enter.
comments.comment: …For when the Only Begotten became one of us, he then also entered into the Holy of Holies through the greater and more perfect tent (Hebrews 9:11–12), that is, into heaven, ‘now to appear in the presence of God for us’ (Hebrews 9:24), as it is written. For it is not himself he sets in the Father’s sight, but us, as in himself, though we had fallen from his presence and, as it were, out of his sight, through the transgression in Adam and the sin that ruled as a tyrant over all. So in Christ we have gained access, and boldness to enter the holy place (Ephesians 3:12; Hebrews 10:19), as wise Paul has told us. For just as we have been raised with him and seated with him in the heavenly places in Christ (Ephesians 2:6), so again in him we have come into the presence of the Father. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Christ gives believers boldness to enter the holy place.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ, our priest, opened the way in for us, entering the Holy of Holies ahead of us as forerunner.
comments.comment: …For we are made perfect nowhere else than in the churches, since it is there, wholly and in every way, that we shall be acceptable to God the Father, with Christ as priest bringing us to him. For through him we have obtained access (Romans 5:2; Ephesians 2:18), and he himself opened for us the way in (Hebrews 10:19–20), entering the Holy of Holies as forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), and showing us the true path. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Paul calls the body of Christ a veil, for the new and living way was opened through his flesh.
comments.comment: …But this much we will say for the present: the veil on four golden pillars with silver bases was then a hint of the mystery of Christ. Why so? Did not the wise Paul also name the body of Christ a veil for us, when he said: ‘the new and living way which he opened for us through the veil, that is, his flesh’ (Hebrews 10:20)? …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the veil in the verse means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The word in which we are cleansed, washing the body with pure water, is the word of faith that confesses Jesus as Lord.
comments.comment: …What then is the word in which we have been cleansed, having washed “the body with pure water,” (Hebrews 10:22) if not altogether that about which the inspired Paul says: “This is the word of faith which we proclaim, that if you confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved; for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation.” (Romans 10:8–10) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Those who know the master's will and do not do it are beaten with many blows, so we receive our stumbles double.
comments.comment: …But it must be said that 'the servant who knew his master’s will and did not do according to his will will be beaten' (Luke 12:47) not with few blows but with 'many.' Therefore it is right that those from the nations who sin receive their sins simply, but that we receive our stumbles double. For 'if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a zeal of fire about to eat the adversaries.' (Hebrews 10:26) …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Setting aside a divine law brings a far heavier charge than sinning against a human.
comments.comment: …“Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has counted the blood of the covenant a common thing, and has insulted the Spirit of grace by which he was sanctified?” (Hebrews 10:28–29) The one who insults — that is, sets aside — a divine law does not face a charge equal to sinning against a human, but one far heavier.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ's blood is not common, so those who count it so fall under a worse sentence.
comments.comment: So the one who has broken the law has fallen under the sentence of death, while the one who has wronged a human might even be worthy of pardon. How, then, is the one who counted Christ’s blood a common thing under a worse sentence than the one who sins against Moses’ law? Yet he is under a worse one — and very fittingly. Christ’s blood is not common, then: for the Word was God, having become flesh (Hebrews 10:28–29). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why counting Christ's blood common brings the worse punishment.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: An apostate does to Jesus spiritually what Jerusalem did to him bodily, by trampling the Son of God.
comments.comment: …And if one is also an apostate, still more does he do to Jesus spiritually what Jerusalem did to him bodily. Therefore: 'How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by the one who has trampled the Son of God and counted common the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?' (Hebrews 10:29) If you have trampled the Son of God and insulted the Spirit of grace, who 'will spare you? Who will look gloomy over you? Who will turn back to ask after the things that make for your peace?' (Jeremiah 15:5) The sinner's soul has betrayed the very Son of God who asked after the things that make for your peace. Who can turn back again and plead concerning peace? …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Faith asks us to believe that God exists, and not to doubt hoped-for things merely because we cannot yet grasp them by knowledge.
comments.comment: …So then, the mystery of theology also seeks assent from unexamined faith. For one must believe, it says, that God exists—not investigate, nor dispute what he is (Hebrews 11:6). And in general, if faith is the substance of things hoped for and the proof of things not seen (Hebrews 11:1), do not be contentious about seeing now the things stored far away, and do not make the things hoped for doubtful because you cannot yet grasp them by knowledge. …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Faith, by which we understand that the ages were prepared by God's word, is a great good that puts away sins and made the fathers well-pleasing.
comments.comment: …By faith we understand that the ages were prepared by the word of God, so that the things seen did not come from the things appearing (Heb 11:3). Faith is, therefore, a truly great and exceptional good. For it is a wealth that puts away sins and a cleansing from every defilement. Furthermore, there is a reminder of that which comes from God; it is a path toward sanctification and sonship, and serves altogether as a reminder of every good thing. In this way, the fathers became well-pleasing, and they possessed a glory that is both bright and unsung. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Enoch was transferred to better things in a way unlike other men, who are parted from their bodies, being taken up or snatched into a divine place.
comments.comment: …The Apostle, having received the word concerning Enoch, says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: 'By faith Enoch was transferred so as not to see death' (Heb 11:5). His life is described in a number of days, and having completed a year and a remainder, he was transferred, which one would logically consider to be a translation into better things, since he was promised the virtue which ought to exist in humans according to perfection and fullness. But his translation did not happen like that of other men; for the bodies of the others, remaining here and being dissolved, were separated from the souls; concerning this it is said that he was transferred, about which we understand that either he was taken up like Elijah or by some other way he was snatched into a divine place. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Enoch's being transferred without seeing death means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Noah, trusting God's command, built the ark to save his household when the flood fell on a corrupted earth.
comments.comment: …Noah, having been charged by faith concerning things not yet seen, stepped forward in piety and was constructing an ark for the salvation of his household. Because the whole earth had destroyed its way, as it is written, and the heart of man has inclined toward evil from youth, God sent a flood upon all the earth. It was like a garden that had been plundered and watered, yet preserved a noble plant within it—the most excellent Noah—so that the human race might be transformed into a new beginning and be saved upon the earth once more. Thus, Noah, having been charged by faith, constructed the ark for the salvation of his house, 'into which a few, that is to say, eight souls were saved through water.' For a decree of death has gone out against all those upon the earth, as they were clearly filled with sin, calling down the Creator into irretrievable wrath. But Noah, being righteous, was being saved universally. For he believed in God, who commanded the construction of the ark; and while the whole earth was baptized, it was carried along by the waters, taking as its pilot God, the Savior of all. …
comments.selected_reason: Tells the verse's story of Noah's faith clearly.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Abraham's offering of Isaac when tested was clear proof of his firmest faith, for he reasoned that God can raise even from the dead.
comments.comment: …To him, when he was already far on in years, the God of all promised a son, quite beyond all expectation, and said that the offspring to come from him would rival the countless multitude of the stars (Genesis 15:5). And because he honored the one who promised, bearing witness to God by this that he can accomplish all things, he was justified before him (Genesis 15:6), and received, as a reward worthy of so God-loving a mind, the forgetting of his former offences. In due course God made the oracle concerning Isaac a trial for the righteous man (Genesis 22:1–2); but in this too he was faithful and loved God, as one who put nothing ahead of his love for God. Yet, as the Savior's disciple says, “Faith was working together with the works, and by the works faith was made firm” (James 2:22). And the admirable Paul himself said somewhere of our forefather Abraham: “By faith he offered up Isaac when he was tested; he who had received the promises was offering up his only son, he to whom it was said, ‘Through Isaac shall your offspring be named’; for he reasoned that God is able even to raise from the dead” (Hebrews 11:17–19). So even if it should perhaps be said that he was justified by works because, when tested, he offered up Isaac, this too was for him a clear proof of the firmest faith. …
comments.selected_reason: Shows how Abraham's offering of Isaac displays faith.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Abraham's faith overcame the storm of testing, for he counted that God is able to raise even from the dead.
comments.comment: …Abraham, who had faith, offered his son Isaac when he was being tested, and this is a great wonder that I am unable to depart from. The blessed Abraham, an old man who was childless, sought an heir from God, and after receiving Isaac, he was commanded to sacrifice him. Abraham's faith was so strong that he overcame the storm of testing, and this is a testament to the stability and safety of holy thoughts, as the most law-abiding Paul will teach, saying Abraham offered Isaac when being tested, having calculated that God is able to raise even from the dead (Hebrews 11:19). Oh, the stability of faith; oh, the safety of holy thoughts; he gave to God the power to accomplish all. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaac set Jacob before Esau by the order of blessing, not of birth.
comments.comment: …By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come (Hebrews 11:20). Previously he set Jacob, then Esau, not according to the sequence of birth, but according to the order of the blessing. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse names Jacob before Esau.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The prophets, chosen for a hard and fearless life, bore stoning, the sword and want for the truth while fixing their gaze on God's unseen things.
comments.comment: …They were chosen by providence to be entrusted with the divine Spirit and the words that come from him because of their way of life: a life hard to imitate, exceedingly strenuous and free, and wholly undaunted in the face of death and danger. For reason, too, shows that the prophets of the God who is over all must be such men. They made the hardihood of Antisthenes, Crates and Diogenes look like a game. At any rate, for the sake of truth and for rebuking sinners freely, “they were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were tempted, they died by the sword; for they went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, ill-treated, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth, men of whom the world on earth was not worthy” (Hebrews 11:37–38). They always fixed their gaze on God and on the invisible things of God, which are not seen by the senses and are for that reason eternal (2 Corinthians 4:18). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the verse's sufferers were and what sustained them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sin of carnal enjoyment is the weight, from which the besetting sin is born.
comments.comment: …Laying aside every weight (Heb 12:1). Sin of carnal enjoyment is a weight, from which the most easily encompassing sin is born. And he said the sin that easily surrounds us and leads us to its own will is 'most easily encompassing'. …
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the weight and the besetting sin are.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Because joy was set before the sinless Christ, he despised the shame of the cross and trampled it.
comments.comment: …Again: 'Who, despising the shame, endured the cross instead of the joy set before him' (Hebrews 12:2). Reproach and shame are the same thing. And see how much it reached him, that joy was set before him, a man not having sin. Therefore he despised the shame, he trampled it. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ endured the cross for the joy set before him in order to destroy the devil and free those enslaved by fear of death.
comments.comment: …For God the Word did not become man for his own sake; and “for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). For what reason? The most wise Paul himself will teach us, saying, “Since the children share in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy him who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery all their lives” (Hebrews 2:14–15). …
comments.selected_reason: Gives the reason Christ endured the cross.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By his resurrection the Son, who voluntarily took the most dishonorable death, was glorified and abolished the shame of his humiliation.
comments.comment: …He [Christ] emptied himself, sitting among us, so that, having overcome death in the flesh, then, having conquered it through the resurrection from the dead, he would declare to us that it is possible to return to life. As the Son of God, he voluntarily took on the most dishonorable and inglorious death, without sparing himself from it, but through his resurrection, he was glorified and abolished the shame and ugliness of his humiliation. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God disciplines in order to transform the disobedient toward what is better, as Scripture says.
comments.comment: …And if we suffer the repayment for these things, either we are disciplined in the present life, as if handed over to torturers (Matthew 18:24–35) by trials and illnesses, or at least we are punished in the age to come. That God disciplines convertibly, transforming the disobedient and hard to lead toward what is better, is easy to see; for divine scripture is full of such things — as in the wise saying, “Whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son he accepts,” (Hebrews 12:6–7) and again, “Endure for discipline,” and what follows.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Affliction lasts only a time, and God's love gives peaceful fruit to those trained by his discipline.
comments.comment: …For even if affliction is necessary for some time, it is not forever; and even if we are justly afflicted on our own account, we ought at least to obtain help according to God’s mercy, so that discipline may give back a peaceful fruit through God’s love for humanity to those who have been trained by it (Hebrews 12:11). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how discipline yields peaceful fruit.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The company of angels is a festival held for the glory of God.
comments.comment: …For a festival and a feast of angels is the one to the glory of God, and to the assembly of firstborns inscribed in the heavens and to God, the judge of all (Heb 12:22-23). …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Holy souls in every city run together to the heavenly Jerusalem as to one mother.
comments.comment: …Yet all these [holy souls in every city] run together, as to one common mother, to the heavenly Jerusalem (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22), the Church of the firstborn (Hebrews 12:23), the fair city above, the true tent which the Lord pitched and not man (Hebrews 8:2). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: The blessed are gathered together there, while sinners are punished by not being together.
comments.comment: …There is a 'church of firstborn enrolled in heaven,' (Hebrews 12:23) where is Mount Zion and city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem. The blessed will be gathered there, that they may be together. But sinners are also punished in this: in not being with one another. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's blood speaks better than Abel's, which cried out against the murderer, because it was poured out as the price for the life of all.
comments.comment: …He [Christ] it is who sanctifies the Church by the sprinkling of his own blood, and does so abundantly. ‘For the priest,’ it says, ‘shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times with his finger before the Lord’ (Leviticus 4:6). ‘For we have come,’ it says, ‘to the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than Abel’ (Hebrews 12:22–24). Abel’s blood cried out to God (Genesis 4:10), condemning the murderer; but the precious blood of Christ, the Savior of us all, speaks better things to God on our behalf, for it was poured out as the price given in exchange for the life of all. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what makes Christ's blood speak better than Abel's.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The one who warned on earth was Moses, but Christ is from heaven, so the sentence is worse for those who turn from him.
comments.comment: …Who is the one who warned on earth, whom the fathers of the Jews refused and so were put in danger? Clearly Moses. But Christ is not from earth; rather from the heavens. For the God Word from above and from the Father became human — and is God. So the sentence is worse for those who turn away from him, and very fittingly. As wise John says: “He who is of the earth speaks from the earth” — that is, human things — “but he who comes from above is above all,” (John 3:31) as God, of course. And that is what Christ was and is. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who warns on earth and who warns from heaven.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The form of this world is removed so eternal things may come, a gift lacking in the law.
comments.comment: …This is what Paul says elsewhere: for he removes the form of this world, so that the temporary things might pass away and the eternal things might come (Heb 12:27). This is, those in the law do not have this gift of which we partake. …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Giving the priests care of those who had suffered most is a type of the churches' care for prisoners.
comments.comment: …He commands that the cities of refuge be entrusted to the Levites, placing in the care of the priests a class of people who had suffered most and who needed the greatest possible help. Here, I think, the churches have a type: to care for prisoners. For ‘Remember,’ it says, ‘those in bonds, as bound with them, and those who are ill-treated, as being yourselves also in the body’ (Hebrews 13:3). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Marriage is honorable and not a sin, since Paul sets it apart from fornication and adultery, which God will judge.
comments.comment: …Now indeed those living according to the Gospel are able to have an honorable marriage and an undefiled bed, as Paul writes to the believers: 'Marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled; but fornicators and adulterers God will judge' (Hebrews 13:4). For by distinguishing the honorable marriage and those using it from fornicators and adulterers, he does not want this to be fornication or adultery; therefore marriage is not even a sin. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly what the verse says about marriage.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Marriage is honorable because the Maker planted in the body a desire for children, so desire that looks only to having children is blameless.
comments.comment: …I mean something like this: “Marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4). For the Maker of all has planted in the nature of the body a movement of appetite that stirs the living creature to the desire for children. For it was said to man, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28); and, he says, “He who formed them in the beginning made them male and female” (Matthew 19:4; Genesis 1:27). So the desire that looks only to having children is blameless; yet as far as the nature of the act goes, the passion would be fleshly, that is, natural. And so it is with the other blameless passions as well. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believers should look to their leaders in order to imitate them, and this looking is praiseworthy.
comments.comment: …Paul writes to the men in Christ: 'perceiving them unto the provocation of love and good works' (Hebrews 10:24) and other things. They perceive in order to imitate them: 'obey' 'those who lead you,' 'who spoke to you the word of God, whose outcome of conduct observing, imitate the faith' (Heb 13:7). Here, perceiving is praiseworthy. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is the same because the Word's unchangeableness by nature remains even when he is understood together with the flesh.
comments.comment: …“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” (Hebrews 13:8) We will find the Word sprung from God called Jesus Christ when he became human from a woman. How, then, is he the same yesterday and today and forever? Clearly by union with the Word from God into one Son, the flesh assumed by him being understood with him. For so the Word’s unchangeableness by nature remains for him even when he is understood with the flesh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Christ can be the same yesterday, today and forever.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ's blood has sanctified us, which shows it is divine and not simply human.
comments.comment: …“Therefore Jesus also, so that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.” (Hebrews 13:12) How would a common human’s blood show us holy? But Christ’s blood has sanctified. So it is divine, then, and not simply human; for God was in flesh, cleansing us by his own blood. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ suffered outside the gate and cleanses the defiled by the death of his flesh, and we must go out to him bearing his reproach.
comments.comment: …He is also the one who suffers outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12), and by the death of his own flesh cleanses those who were defiled. For ‘the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled on those who are defiled,’ it says, ‘sanctify for the purification of the flesh’ (Hebrews 9:13). So Emmanuel, being one and the same, gives off his fragrance in the holy tents, I mean the churches, and he also suffered outside the gate; and there, as the inspired Paul said, we too must go out, bearing his reproach (Hebrews 13:13). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ suffered for us outside the gate, and we too go out bearing his reproach, dying to the world and offering our souls as a sacrifice.
comments.comment: …For in a way, as if in the likeness of the victims, we offer up our own souls in sacrifice and bring them to God. We die to the world and to minding the things of the flesh (Romans 8:5), we endure the putting to death of the passions, and we are all but crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:19–20), so that, passing over to a holy and blameless life, we may live as he wills. The inspired Paul, too, writes something of this kind: ‘Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our body’ (2 Corinthians 4:10). And again: ‘If we endure, we shall also reign with him’ (2 Timothy 2:12). If we are conformed to his death and his sufferings, as it is written, we shall share in the resurrection and the glory as well (Philippians 3:10–11). So then Christ suffered for us outside the gate, as the blessed Paul says, and we too go out of the gate, bearing his reproach (Hebrews 13:12–13); slain in the same way, like a young calf, and burned whole like a ram, we make our life in Christ fragrant to God. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what going out to Christ outside the gate means for believers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: God is pleased with the spiritual sacrifices of holy souls in every land: faith, hope, love, endurance, meekness and love for the poor.
comments.comment: …But the law, as I think, seems again to hint at something mystical. For there are countless regions and cities throughout the whole world in which holy and God-loving human souls serve God by living lawfully and conducting their lives according to the Gospel, offering to him, as it were, sacrifices for a fragrant aroma (a spiritual one, clearly): faith, hope, love, endurance, meekness and love for the poor. ‘For with such sacrifices God is well pleased’ (Hebrews 13:16), as the Scriptures say. …
comments.selected_reason: Says what the sacrifices of this verse are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13
